title: Concurrency Pitfalls
subtitle: Stale responses, abort, unhandled rejections, forEach

cards.front: Does single-threaded JS still have concurrency?
cards.meaning: Yes — many async operations can be in flight at once. The danger is usually not multi-threaded memory races. Two operations start; the older one finishes after the newer one and still updates UI/state. Send order ≠ completion order: the event loop runs whichever callback becomes ready first.

Classic stale-fetch / completion-order race: two requests in flight; latency doesn't preserve send order; response for 'a' may arrive after 'ab' and overwrite state. Same family: tab switching, rapid filter changes, React effect re-runs without cleanup, double-clicked submit, Nest shared mutable cache without versioning.
cards.example: type a → request A; type ab → request B; B returns setResults(ab); A returns setResults(a) — stale wins

cards.meaning: Keep a monotonically increasing generation (or latest query). Increment on each new request; after await, only setState if id === latest. React effect equivalent: let cancelled = false; cleanup sets cancelled = true; ignore then/setState when cancelled. Stops applying stale data; doesn't cancel network unless paired with abort. Wasted bandwidth/CPU may continue.
cards.example: let latest = 0; const id = ++latest; const results = await fetchResults(query); if (id !== latest) return;

cards.meaning: Abort previous controller when a new query starts; pass signal to fetch. abort() signals all consumers of that signal; fetch rejects with AbortError / DOMException. Treat abort as expected control flow, not a user-facing failure (noisy toasts on every keystroke). Reduces wasted work vs ignore-only.

Abort stops/cancels in-flight I/O where supported; ignore-stale only prevents bad UI updates. Abort reduces waste; a generation check still helps if some APIs can't abort or if multiple code paths can set state. Use both when needed. Search/typeahead: debounce + AbortController (+ ignore-stale). Effect load by id: abort or cancelled flag in cleanup.

cards.front: Why React Query / SWR / RTK Query exist?
cards.meaning: They automate query keys + cancellation / ignore stale. Knowing the manual pattern (request id + AbortController) proves you understand why they exist — don't rely only on library magic without being able to explain query keys / cancel.

cards.front: What is an unhandled Promise rejection?
cards.meaning: A Promise rejects and nothing handles it in time — no .catch, no await inside try/catch on a caller that actually waits. Fire-and-forget async that throws is a typical leak. Node: warnings; can crash depending on version / --unhandled-rejections. Browsers/RN: easy to miss; silent failed features.
cards.example: async function risky() { throw new Error('boom'); } risky(); // unhandled rejection risk

cards.meaning: Be awaited in try/catch or have an explicit .catch(). Fire-and-forget only when deliberate and visible — still prefer .catch(logError). Example: void saveDraft(data).catch(logError) for an intentional background save.

cards.front: Why is async onclick a common leak?
cards.meaning: button.onclick = async () => { await submit(); } — rejection becomes unhandled unless try/catch inside. Event handlers must catch or route errors to UI.

cards.front: items.forEach(async item => await save(item)); then log done?
cards.meaning: done runs before saves finish — forEach expects a sync visitor and ignores returned Promises. All async visitors start; their Promises float away (often unhandled if save rejects).
cards.example: items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); }); console.log('done'); // done first

cards.meaning: Sequential: for (const item of items) await save(item). Parallel: await Promise.all(items.map(item => save(item))). Partial OK: await Promise.allSettled(...). Limited concurrency: pool / batch helper. Bulk save: all / allSettled / pool — not forEach + async.
You get an array of Promises — must await Promise.all (or allSettled) if you need completion or error handling as one unit. Avoid map(async) without combining if you need completion.

Debounce: run after activity settles (typeahead wait until typing pauses) — fewer starts. Throttle: at most once per interval while activity continues (scroll, resize) — caps rate of starts. Both reduce in-flight async work and race surface. Neither replaces abort/ignore-stale if a slow response can still outrun a later one. Debounce the async start, not only the render — fetch on every keypress still creates races.

cards.front: React Strict Mode / effect re-run pitfall?
cards.meaning: Effects may mount→cleanup→mount in dev. Without cleanup (cancelled = true / abort), you double-fetch and risk races.
Two clicks → two POSTs. Disable the button, use idempotency keys, or an in-flight guard: if (inFlight) return; inFlight = true; try { await submit(); } finally { inFlight = false; }.

cards.front: Shared mutable state in Nest — race?
cards.meaning: Concurrent requests on one Node process share module-level variables. A request-scoped latest flag on a singleton service can cross wires — prefer per-request locals, not globals, for cancellation tokens.
